Let me carefully check this proof.

The problem: sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ of integers $> 1$, where $a_{n+1}$ is the smallest integer greater than $a_n$ with $\gcd(a_{n+1}, a_i) > 1$ for all $i \le n$. Prove the sequence is eventually... actually exactly "linearly periodic": $a_{n+T} = a_n + L$.

The write-up:

Step 1: Lemma 1 (pairwise non-coprimality) — correct, immediate from definition.

Lemma 2 (completeness): $S = \{m \ge a_1 : \gcd(m, s) > 1 \ \forall s \in S\}$. The "$\supseteq$" direction: Let $m \ge a_1$ with $\gcd(m, s) > 1$ for all $s \in S$, suppose $m \notin S$. Then $m > a_1$... wait, why $m > a_1$? Since $m \ge a_1$ and $m \ne a_1$ (as $a_1 \in S$ and $m \notin S$), $m > a_1$. Good. Define $n = \max\{i : a_i < m\}$ — well-defined since $a_1 < m$. Then $a_{n+1} \ge m$ and $a_{n+1} \ne m$ since $m \notin S$; so $a_{n+1} > m$. But $m > a_n$ and $\gcd(m, a_i) > 1$ for all $i \le n$, so $m$ is a candidate for $a_{n+1}$; minimality gives $a_{n+1} \le m$. Contradiction. Correct.

Lemma 3 (downward witnesses): If $m > a_1$ and $m \notin S$, then exists $s \in S$, $s < m$, $\gcd(s, m) = 1$. Proof: $n = \max\{i : a_i < m\}$; then $a_n < m < a_{n+1}$. If $\gcd(m, a_i) > 1$ for all $i \le n$, then $m$ is a candidate, so $a_{n+1} \le m$, contradiction. Hence some $i \le n$ with $\gcd(m, a_i) = 1$; $s = a_i \le a_n < m$. Correct.

Wait, one subtlety: $n = \max\{i \ge 1: a_i < m\}$ requires $m > a_1$; yes that's assumed. And $a_{n+1} > m$: since $a_{n+1} \ge m$ by maximality (if $a_{n+1} < m$ then $n+1$ would be in the set). Actually maximality gives $a_{n+1} \ge m$. Then $a_{n+1} = m$ would mean $m \in S$, contradiction; so $a_{n+1} > m$. Good.

Step 2: Transversals. Definition: prime set $X$ is a transversal if $X \cap P(s) \ne \emptyset$ for every $s \in S$. A member is a minimal transversal (inclusion-minimal). $d_Q = \pi(Q)$ = product of primes in $Q$.

Remark: every transversal contains a member: finite subsets argument — among subsets of $X$ that are transversals (nonempty collection since $X$ itself is a transversal; finitely many subsets), choose inclusion-minimal one; any proper subset that is a transversal is a subset of $X$, contradicting minimality. Correct.

Lemma 4: $m \in S \iff d_Q \mid m$ for some member $Q$ (for $m \ge a_1$).

"$\Leftarrow$": $d_Q \mid m$ means $Q \subseteq P(m)$ (by (0), since $d_Q$ is squarefree product). Then for every $s \in S$, $Q \cap P(s) \ne \emptyset$, so $P(m) \cap P(s) \ne \emptyset$, so $\gcd(m, s) > 1$. Then Lemma 2 gives $m \in S$ (using $m \ge a_1$). Correct.

"$\Rightarrow$": $m \in S$, then $P(m)$ is a transversal (by Lemma 1 applied to $s = m$: $\gcd(m, s') > 1$ for all $s' \in S$, so $P(m) \cap P(s') \ne \emptyset$). Then contains a member $Q \subseteq P(m)$, so $d_Q \mid m$. Correct.

$\mathcal M \ne \emptyset$: $P(a_1)$ is a transversal, contains a member. Correct.

Lemma 5: members pairwise intersect. Choose distinct primes $p, p' \notin Q \cup Q'$; integers $e, e' \ge 1$ with $m = d_Q p^e \ge a_1$, $m' = d_{Q'} p'^{e'} \ge a_1$. By Lemma 4 "$\Leftarrow$", $m, m' \in S$. Note: $P(m) = Q \cup \{p\}$ — yes since $d_Q$ is squarefree. Lemma 1: $\gcd(m, m') > 1$, so some prime $u \in P(m) \cap P(m') = (Q \cup \{p\}) \cap (Q' \cup \{p'\})$. Since $p \ne p'$, $p \notin Q'$ (choice of $p \notin Q \cup Q'$), $p' \notin Q$. So $u \in Q \cap Q'$. Correct. Note if $Q = Q'$, trivial anyway; the argument works.

Step 3: Lemma 6 (cheap witness). Let $Q \in \mathcal M$ with $|Q| \ge 2$, $t \in Q$. Then exists $Q' \in \mathcal M$ with $Q' \cap Q = \{t\}$ and $d_{Q'} < a_1 d_Q / t$.

Proof: $X = Q \setminus \{t\}$, $\pi(X) = d_Q / t \ge 2$. No member is a subset of $X$: if $M \subseteq X \subsetneq Q$ and $M$ is a transversal, contradicts minimality of member $Q$. Correct.

Let $e \ge 1$ minimal with $m = \pi(X)^e > a_1$. Then $m \le a_1 \pi(X)$: if $e = 1$, $m = \pi(X) \le a_1 \pi(X)$ (since $a_1 \ge 2 \ge 1$). If $e \ge 2$, $\pi(X)^{e-1} \le a_1$ so $m \le a_1 \pi(X)$. Correct.

$P(m) = X$ (since $\pi(X)$ squarefree, $m$ is a power of a squarefree number, so $P(m) = X$). $X$ contains no member, $m > a_1$, so Lemma 4 gives $m \notin S$. Lemma 3: exists $s \in S$, $s < m$, $\gcd(s, m) = 1$, i.e. $P(s) \cap X = \emptyset$. Then by Lemma 4 "$\Rightarrow$", exists member $Q' \subseteq P(s)$. Then $Q' \cap X = \emptyset$ (since $Q' \subseteq P(s)$ and $P(s) \cap X = \emptyset$). And $d_{Q'} \mid s$ (since $Q' \subseteq P(s)$, (0)), so $d_{Q'} \le s < m \le a_1 \pi(X) = a_1 d_Q / t$. By Lemma 5, $Q' \cap Q \ne \emptyset$; since $Q = X \cup \{t\}$ and $Q' \cap X = \emptyset$, $Q' \cap Q = \{t\}$. Correct.

One subtle point: Lemma 3 requires $m > a_1$, which holds. Also $m \notin S$ requires Lemma 4's "$\Rightarrow$" direction: $m \in S$ would imply some member $Q'' \mid m$, i.e., $Q'' \subseteq P(m) = X$, contradicting no member subset of $X$. Correct.

Step 4: Lemma 7: every prime in a member is $\le a_1$.

Case A: some member is singleton $\{p\}$. For any $M \in \mathcal M$, $M \cap \{p\} \ne \emptyset$ by Lemma 5, so $p \in M$. Then $\{p\} \subseteq M$ is a transversal, so by minimality $M = \{p\}$. Hence $\mathcal M = \{\{p\}\}$. $a_1 \in S$, so some member divides $a_1$: $d_Q \mid a_1$ where $Q = \{p\}$, so $p \mid a_1$, $p \le a_1$. Correct.

Case B: every member has $\ge 2$ elements. Suppose some member $Q_0$ contains prime $q > a_1$. Define recursively $Q_{i+1}$ = member from Lemma 6 applied to $Q_i$, $t = q$. Induction: $q \in Q_i$ for $i = 0$ by assumption; for $i \ge 1$, $Q_i \cap Q_{i-1} = \{q\}$ so $q \in Q_i$. Also $|Q_i| \ge 2$ by Case B hypothesis. Lemma 6: $d_{Q_{i+1}} < (a_1/q) d_{Q_i}$, so $d_{Q_i} < (a_1/q)^i d_{Q_0}$. Since $a_1/q < 1$, $d_{Q_i} \to 0$; but $d_{Q_i} \ge q \ge 2$. Contradiction. Correct.

Wait: we need $Q_{i+1} \ne Q_i$? Actually Lemma 6 gives $Q' \cap Q = \{t\}$; if $Q' = Q$ then $Q \cap Q = Q = \{t\}$, i.e., $|Q| = 1$, contradicting $|Q| \ge 2$. So $Q_{i+1} \ne Q_i$ automatically; but actually we don't even need that: the descent $d_{Q_{i+1}} < (a_1/q) d_{Q_i}$ with $a_1/q < 1$ forces strict decrease anyway, so even if we picked any member satisfying the conclusion, it's fine. The recursion is well-defined (exists by Lemma 6). Correct.

Hmm, but actually there's a subtle point: Lemma 6 requires $|Q| \ge 2$. In Case B all members have $\ge 2$ elements. Good.

Lemma 8: finiteness. Every member is a subset of $\Pi = \{p \le a_1\}$, finite, so $\mathcal M$ finite. Correct.

Step 5: Conclusion. $M = \prod_{p \le a_1} p$, $R = \{r \in \{0, \ldots, M-1\} : d_Q \mid r \text{ for some } Q\}$, $T = |R|$, $L = M$. $0 \in R$ so $T \ge 1$. Since $d_Q \mid M$ for all $Q$ (each $d_Q$ is a product of distinct primes $\le a_1$, hence divides $M$), we have $d_Q \mid m \iff d_Q \mid (m \bmod M)$. So (3): $m \in S \iff (m \bmod M) \in R$ for $m \ge a_1$. Then (4): $m \in S \iff m + M \in S$ for $m \ge a_1$.

Hmm, careful with (4): $m + M \ge a_1$ always; and $m + M \equiv m \pmod M$, so (3) applies to both if both $\ge a_1$. For $m \ge a_1$: $m \in S \iff (m \bmod M) \in R \iff ((m+M) \bmod M) \in R \iff m + M \in S$. Correct.

Blocks $I_k = \{a_1 + kM, \ldots, a_1 + (k+1)M - 1\}$. Each contains one representative of each residue class mod $M$. By (3), $|S \cap I_k| = T$ for all $k$. Correct.

Claim: elements of $S$ smaller than $a_1 + kM$ are exactly $a_1, \ldots, a_{kT}$; induction: base $k = 0$: elements of $S$ smaller than $a_1$: none, and $a_1, \ldots, a_0$ is empty. Inductive step: elements smaller than $a_1 + (k+1)M$ = (elements smaller than $a_1 + kM$, i.e. $a_1, \ldots, a_{kT}$) together with $S \cap I_k$ (elements in $[a_1 + kM, a_1 + (k+1)M - 1]$). Note: elements of $S$ smaller than $a_1 + (k+1)M$ are those $< a_1 + kM$ plus those in $[a_1 + kM, a_1 + (k+1)M)$, which is $I_k$. Since $S \cap I_k$ has $T$ elements, total $(k+1)T$. Each element of $S \cap I_k$ exceeds $a_1 + kM >$ all elements below $a_1 + kM$... wait, elements of $S \cap I_k$ are $\ge a_1 + kM$, and elements of $S$ below $a_1 + kM$ are $< a_1 + kM$. So indeed the $I_k$ elements come after. Since $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ enumerates $S$ increasingly, $S \cap I_k = \{a_{kT+1}, \ldots, a_{(k+1)T}\}$. Correct.

Then $\varphi: m \mapsto m + M$ maps $S \cap I_k$ into $S \cap I_{k+1}$ bijectively (mutually inverse maps with $m' \mapsto m' - M$). A strictly increasing bijection between finite ordered sets matches $j$-th smallest to $j$-th smallest. So $a_{(k+1)T + j} = a_{kT + j} + M$ for $k \ge 0$, $1 \le j \le T$.

Then for any $n \ge 1$, write $n = kT + j$, $0 \le k$, $1 \le j \le T$ (division algorithm), so $a_{n+T} = a_n + M = a_n + L$. Correct.

Hmm wait, one point: is $\varphi$ strictly increasing bijection matching the $j$-th smallest of $S\cap I_k$ to the $j$-th smallest of $S \cap I_{k+1}$? Yes: $m \mapsto m + M$ is increasing, and it's a bijection between the two sets (injective trivially; surjective by inverse map). The $j$-th smallest element of $S \cap I_k$ maps to an element of $S \cap I_{k+1}$ that has exactly $j-1$ elements of $S\cap I_{k+1}$ below it (images of the smaller ones), so it's the $j$-th smallest. Correct.

Also we need each $S \cap I_k$ to be nonempty for the enumeration to make sense; $T \ge 1$ ensures it. Actually the claim enumerates $a_{kT+1}, \ldots, a_{(k+1)T}$ — fine.

Let me double check the key inequality in Lemma 6: $d_{Q'} < a_1 d_Q / t$. We have $d_{Q'} \le s < m \le a_1 \pi(X) = a_1 d_Q / t$. Strict inequality: $d_{Q'} \le s$ and $s < m$, so $d_{Q'} < m \le a_1 \pi(X)$. So $d_{Q'} < a_1 d_Q / t$. Correct. Actually the chain gives $d_{Q'} < m \le a_1\pi(X)$, so $d_{Q'} < a_1 \pi(X)$ only if $d_{Q'} < a_1 \pi(X)$; since $d_{Q'} < m \le a_1\pi(X)$, indeed $d_{Q'} < a_1\pi(X)$. Good.

Also note: in Lemma 6, $m = \pi(X)^e$ with minimal $e \ge 1$ such that $m > a_1$. Since $\pi(X) \ge 2$, such $e$ exists. Also we need $P(m) = X$: $m = \pi(X)^e$, and $\pi(X)$ is a product of distinct primes, so $P(m) = X$. Correct.

Edge cases: What if $Q \setminus \{t\} = \emptyset$? Then Lemma 6 requires $|Q| \ge 2$ so $X \ne \emptyset$. Good.

What about the case $a_1 = 2$? Then $S$: $a_1 = 2$. Members: transversals of $\{P(s)\}$. Since all elements of $S$ are pairwise non-coprime and $2 \in S$, every $s \in S$ is even. Then $S = \{m \ge 2 : \gcd(m, s) > 1 \forall s \in S\} = \{m \ge 2 \text{ even}\} = 2\mathbb Z_{\ge 2}$. So $a_n = 2n$. Check: $a_2 = 4$: smallest integer $> 2$ sharing factor with 2 is 4. Yes. Members: $\{\{2\}\}$, singleton. Case A of Lemma 7. $M = 2$, $R = \{0\}$, $T = 1$, $L = 2$: $a_{n+1} = a_n + 2$. Correct.

Also check that Lemma 3's proof handles $n$ well: $m > a_1$ so $n \ge 1$ exists. Good.

Now let me verify the claim "$d_Q \mid m \iff d_Q \mid (m \bmod M)$" — since $d_Q \mid M$, $m \equiv m \bmod M \pmod{d_Q}$, so yes.

Also, the "union of arithmetic progressions" characterization: $S = [a_1, \infty) \cap \bigcup_Q d_Q \mathbb Z$. This is exactly Lemma 4 combined with finiteness.

Overall the proof looks complete and correct. Let me scrutinize potential gaps:

1. In Lemma 2's "$\supseteq$", the argument needs $\gcd(m, a_i) > 1$ for $i \le n$ — yes since all $a_i \in S$ and hypothesis. And $m > a_n$? We need $m$ to be a candidate: integer greater than $a_n$ with gcd condition. $m > a_n$ since $a_n < m$ by definition of $n$. Good.

2. In Lemma 3, similar.

3. Lemma 5: need $e, e'$ such that $m, m' \ge a_1$ — exists since $p, p'$ can be raised to large powers. Also $p, p'$ distinct primes not in $Q \cup Q'$ — infinitely many primes. Good. Also note: need $P(m) = Q \cup \{p\}$ — yes.

4. Lemma 7 Case A: "$\mathcal M = \{\{p\}\}$" — for any member $M'$, $p \in M'$ by Lemma 5 (with the singleton member $\{p\}$). Then $\{p\} \subseteq M'$ is a transversal (subset of transversal... wait, a superset of a transversal is a transversal; $\{p\}$ is a transversal since it's a member, so any superset is a transversal). Minimality of $M'$ as a member: a member is a transversal with no proper subset a transversal. $\{p\} \subseteq M'$ is a transversal; if $\{p\} \subsetneq M'$, contradiction with member minimality. So $M' = \{p\}$. Correct. Then apply Lemma 4 "$\Rightarrow$" to $a_1 \in S$: some member $Q$ with $d_Q \mid a_1$; $Q = \{p\}$, so $p \mid a_1$, $p \le a_1$. Correct.

5. Case B induction: at each step, Lemma 6 applied to $Q_i$ with $t = q$ requires $q \in Q_i$ and $|Q_i| \ge 2$. Base: $q \in Q_0$ by assumption, $|Q_0| \ge 2$ by Case B. Step: $Q_{i+1} \cap Q_i = \{q\}$, so $q \in Q_{i+1}$; and $|Q_{i+1}| \ge 2$ by Case B hypothesis (it's a member). Good. Descent: $d_{Q_{i+1}} < (a_1/q) d_{Q_i}$. Since $q > a_1 \ge 2$, ratio $< 1$. Then $d_{Q_i} \to 0$ but each $d_{Q_i} \ge q \ge 2$ (as $q \in Q_i$, and $d$ is product of distinct primes including $q$; $d_{Q_i} \ge q$). Contradiction. Correct.

6. Step 5's final: every positive integer $n$ can be uniquely written $n = kT + j$ with $k \ge 0$, $1 \le j \le T$. Yes.

Also need: the blocks $I_k$ cover all of $[a_1, \infty)$: $\bigcup_{k \ge 0} I_k = [a_1, \infty)$. Yes.

One more check: In the claim, "$S \cap I_k$ ... each larger than every element of $S$ below $a_1 + kM$". Elements of $S \cap I_k$ are $\ge a_1 + kM$. Elements of $S$ below $a_1 + kM$ are $< a_1 + kM$. Fine.

Potential subtle issue: In Lemma 4 "$\Rightarrow$", they use Lemma 1 which says $P(m)$ is a transversal for $m \in S$ — i.e., $P(m) \cap P(s) \ne \emptyset$ for all $s \in S$, i.e. $\gcd(m, s) > 1$ for all $s \in S$, which is Lemma 1. Good.

The write-up also includes a preamble ("tracking file") with status "solved" and descriptions of approaches. The "Full proof" section contains the actual proof. The proof appears complete and rigorous.

Let me double-check the numerical claims aren't needed — they're just remarks; the proof stands on its own.

One more check on Lemma 6: "no member is a subset of $X$". Suppose $M \subseteq X \subsetneq Q$, $M \in \mathcal M$. Then $M$ is a transversal, proper subset of $Q$, contradicting $Q$ being a member (minimal transversal). Correct.

And in Lemma 6, the conclusion $Q' \cap Q = \{t\}$: $Q' \cap Q \neq \emptyset$ by Lemma 5, and $Q' \cap Q \subseteq (Q' \cap X) \cup (Q' \cap \{t\}) = \emptyset \cup (Q' \cap \{t\})$. So $Q' \cap Q \subseteq \{t\}$ and nonempty, so $= \{t\}$. Correct.

Also, is there an issue if $Q' = Q$? Then $Q' \cap Q = Q$, which would need $Q = \{t\}$, but $|Q| \ge 2$. So $Q' \ne Q$ automatically. Not needed though.

Everything checks out. The proof is complete, rigorous, and self-contained. The structure: greediness → self-describing set $S$ → $S$ is union of residue classes modulo finitely many squarefree moduli with primes $\le a_1$ → periodicity from the start.

Now grading: This is a 7. Complete and correct proof.

Main gap: none.

Notes: Verify once more whether there might be an issue with $T$ when $R$ includes residue classes... $T \geq 1$ since $0 \in R$. Fine.

Actually, let me reconsider Lemma 3's use: it requires $m \notin S$ and $m > a_1$. In Lemma 6, $m = \pi(X)^e > a_1$ and $m \notin S$ by Lemma 4 contrapositive: if $m \in S$ then some member $Q'' \subseteq P(m) = X$ — contradicts no member $\subseteq X$. Correct.

Also, "each $d_Q$ is a product of distinct primes $\le a_1$, hence divides $M$": $M$ is the product of all primes $\le a_1$, each to the first power; $d_Q$ is squarefree with all prime factors $\le a_1$; so $d_Q \mid M$. Correct.

Thus grade 7, complete true, main_gap "none".
